New startup enables drivers to autonomously surveil other drivers to build up a distributed profile of all drivers and their driving habits. If a known bad driver is detected, it can warn you.

The software has already been in live testing in New York City and Silicon Valley. If you've been driving around those cities your driving habits have most likely been recorded and analyzed. I think this is an interesting and inevitable new paradigm. People often worry about the government surveiling them, but private companies in distributed efforts with users can do just as much if not more.

Yet another reason that I think people need to stop trying to pretend technology isn't going to go this route and instead look for tougher protections for privacy rights and rules regarding data collection. For instance should this software catch on - if you ever engage in, for instance, speeding or running a red light - there's a good chance it was just detected and logged. Should the police be able to subpoena the company demanding a list of all individuals that have broken traffic laws?

I'd say the police shouldn't be allowed to turn the company into an arm of law enforcement. It's bad business for the company, and damages their reputation needlessly. We're all going to end up surveilled 24/7 anyways eventually, but it should come with protections and limitations. For example, eventually when we all have AI chips in our heads, the AI chip should have no ability to independently connect to outside networks or be connected to. You can say that on one hand, that is the end of privacy, but on the other hand you have a computer in your brain and all the benefits of that as well as a second perspective on all the things you do or think immediately available including the better planning that would give.

When it comes to the specific example in the OP, there definitely needs to be protections for the sake of both the business and the drivers. Someone who chronically speeds can be treated as a dangerous driver, but only in the case that a crash is caused should the police be allowed to take the data from the surrounding cams to watch the crash take place, and the evidence from that should ONLY be allowed to be used for the crash. Otherwise, without heavy restrictions on interaction with police, it will be extremely difficult for the business to receive trust in the long term, and the only way they'd be able to grow larger as a company is for use of the product to be required by law via fining those who don't make use of it.(ayy lmao ACA) That's an extremely heavy-handed way of doing it, and would result in everyone not the company or the government being extremely unhappy at minimum with riots being far more likely. There would also never be any trust in a business doing something similar, and I'd say National Security Letters are the real problem here. They need to be properly handled, or it will be impossible for a properly informed person to ever trust a company like this as long as it's based in the US. There's also the problem of the NSA and co. scraping everything they possibly can from any packets that flow over the WWW, requiring this to have extremely strong crypto at minimum.

My current thoughts are that in the current state of the world this is a thing that can't be allowed to catch on. We have to change government policies first by actually getting people to use the rights they have as citizens and dumping the politicians we currently have and elevating people who actually care. The problem with this is that it isn't going to happen.

There's even trickier questions. Should the company be allowed to voluntarily give the police data? That opens up the possibility of the company charging "administrative data processing fees." The administrative data processing fee is calculated in a strange way. In cases where they have evidence of a crime that would result in a fine of $300, the fee is $150. In cases where the fine would be $100, their administrative data processing fee would be $50.

Unfortunately I don't think corporate trust is really going to matter. Imagine this app was freely available and you could up it up and get a real time stream of information about all the drivers around you and their reckless (or not) driving habits. Would you? I think most anybody would. Even if not out of immediate utility, it'd just be plain interesting. Eventually we'll also see the same thing for people - click on your app, look around and get dynamic information about all the people around you (while helping to create even more). And this is really going to suck in the current wild west of digital privacy that we currently have.

I would recommend requiring that we can publicly see the action of selling data. It should be required to be in a fairly prominent and easily accessible location on their website. We shouldn't be able to see the data sold, but we should be allowed to know that it's taking place, and should be alerted when the data sold is related to you. This should be enough to let us know that we can't afford to trust them, and if our self-control is that bad then at least we know what we're doing to ourselves.
